voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.
title: Kinematics applications: relative motion, projectiles and circles

sources.title: NTA: JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 2

chapters.title: Vectors and the moving observer
chapters.formula: v(A relative to B) = v(A) - v(B)
points: Choose axes; subtract corresponding velocity components.
18 m/s and 12 m/s east: closing speed is 6 m/s.
A 120 m gap closes in 20 s; full train passage needs both lengths.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. You already know how to describe motion along a straight line. Today we let motion turn corners, change observers, and leave the ground. Our tools are still position, velocity, acceleration, and time. We just need to keep direction in the picture. Choose east as positive x and north as positive y. A velocity with components three meters per second east and four north has speed five, not seven. The components are perpendicular, so their squared values add. The direction is about fifty-three degrees north of east. Components carry signs; the speed is the nonnegative magnitude. Now imagine watching a faster bus from a slower bus. The ground measures their velocities as eighteen and twelve meters per second east. What speed does the slower bus see? Take a moment. Six meters per second east. Relative position means the position of A minus the position of B. Differentiating that difference gives relative velocity: velocity of A minus velocity of B. This subtraction works component by component, not just along a road. If the faster vehicle starts one hundred twenty meters behind the slower one and both velocities stay constant, that gap closes at six meters per second. Catch-up time is one hundred twenty divided by six, or twenty seconds. If B instead moves west at twelve, its signed velocity is negative twelve. Subtracting it gives thirty meters per second east. The familiar add-the-speeds shortcut is really signed vector subtraction. For two trains travelling east at eighteen and twelve, with lengths one hundred and one hundred forty meters, complete overtaking from first overlap to last overlap requires two hundred forty meters of relative travel. That takes forty seconds, assuming parallel tracks and constant velocities. A point catching a point and a whole train passing another train are different geometry questions. In a JEE-style problem, draw the initial separation before choosing what distance to divide by relative speed.

chapters.title: River crossing: fastest is not straight across
points: River east at 3 m/s; boat speed relative to water is 5 m/s.
Aim north: cross 120 m in 24 s, drifting 72 m east.
Land opposite: aim upstream; north component is 4 m/s, time 30 s.
chapters.script: Let's take the same observer idea to a river. Here is our original example. The banks are one hundred twenty meters apart, measured northward. Water flows east at three meters per second. A boat can maintain five meters per second relative to the water. Ignore changes in current and the time taken to turn. The boat's ground velocity is its velocity relative to water plus the water's velocity relative to ground. Picture walking across a moving walkway: your own motion and the walkway's motion both contribute. First, aim the boat due north. The ground velocity then has a north component of five and an east component of three. Crossing time depends on the north component because that is the direction of the river's width. One hundred twenty divided by five gives twenty-four seconds. During that time, the current carries the boat seventy-two meters east. This is the minimum crossing time for the given boat speed and a current parallel to the banks. Why? The largest possible north component of a five-meter-per-second velocity is five. Any upstream tilt makes that component smaller. Now change the goal. We want to reach the point directly opposite our starting point. Should we still aim north? Think about the current for a moment. No. Aim upstream so the boat's westward component relative to water is three meters per second. It cancels the current's eastward three. The boat's own speed is still five, so its north component is the square root of twenty-five minus nine: four meters per second. The crossing now takes thirty seconds. The upstream heading makes about thirty-seven degrees with north, since sine of that angle is three divided by five. Minimum time and zero drift are different instructions, not competing answers to the same question. In this ideal model, directly opposite landing requires boat speed greater than current speed. Equal speeds leave no north component when the current is canceled. Read the requested destination before calculating, and always label the frame of each velocity.

chapters.title: Projectiles: two directions, one clock
chapters.formula: x = ux t; y = uy t - gt^2/2; vy = uy - gt
points: Uniform gravity downward; air resistance ignored.
ux = u cos(theta); uy = u sin(theta); acceleration is (0, -g).
u = 20 m/s at 30 degrees, g = 10: T = 2 s, H = 5 m, R = 20 sqrt(3) m.
chapters.script: A ball follows a curved path, but our equations do not have to become mysterious. Split its motion into horizontal and vertical components. We assume a uniform downward gravitational field and neglect air resistance. After launch, gravity is the only acceleration. Choose the launch point as origin, positive x horizontally, and positive y upward. For speed u at angle theta above the horizontal, the initial horizontal component is u times cosine theta. The vertical component is u times sine theta. Horizontal acceleration is zero, so horizontal velocity stays constant. Vertical acceleration is negative g, so vertical velocity changes. Both directions share the same elapsed time. That is what connects them. Horizontal displacement is the initial horizontal component multiplied by time. Vertical displacement is the initial vertical component multiplied by time, minus one half g times time squared. Let's launch an ideal ball at twenty meters per second, thirty degrees above horizontal. Use g equal to ten meters per second squared for this example. Its horizontal component is ten square root of three, and its vertical component is ten. At the top, vertical velocity becomes zero. Ten minus ten times t equals zero, giving one second to reach the top. Has the ball stopped? Take a moment. Only its vertical component has stopped. Its horizontal velocity is still ten square root of three. Acceleration is still ten downward. The maximum height above launch is ten squared divided by twice ten, or five meters. If the ball lands at its launch height, the nonzero root of zero equals ten t minus five t squared is two seconds. Multiply that time by the horizontal component to get a range of twenty square root of three meters, about thirty-four point six. Eliminating time gives a downward-opening parabolic trajectory. The curve comes from horizontal motion proportional to time and vertical motion containing time squared. For same-height landing, time of flight is twice u sine theta divided by g, and range is u squared sine twice theta divided by g. Those shortcuts require the stated ideal model and equal launch and landing heights. They are not universal projectile formulas.

chapters.title: Different heights: solve the landing condition
chapters.formula: Horizontal launch: t = sqrt(2h/g); range = ux t
points: Height and horizontal speed answer different parts of the problem.
Launch horizontally at 15 m/s from h = 20 m, g = 10: t = 2 s, range = 30 m.
Impact velocity is (15, -20) m/s; speed is 25 m/s.
chapters.script: Now the landing point is below the launch point. This is where memorized same-height formulas can quietly give the wrong answer. Imagine an ideal horizontal launch at fifteen meters per second from a platform twenty meters above the landing surface. Use g equal to ten and ignore air resistance. Put the origin at launch and keep upward positive. Initial vertical velocity is zero. At landing, y is negative twenty, not positive twenty. Our vertical equation becomes negative twenty equals negative five t squared. Time is two seconds; discard the negative root because we are asking about the event after launch. Horizontal displacement is fifteen times two, or thirty meters. Notice why increasing horizontal launch speed would increase range without changing falling time in this ideal model. The vertical drop and vertical initial velocity have not changed. At impact, horizontal velocity is still positive fifteen. Vertical velocity is negative twenty. The speed is the square root of fifteen squared plus twenty squared, giving twenty-five meters per second. The direction is about fifty-three degrees below horizontal. We do not add fifteen and twenty as scalar speeds. Those components are perpendicular. For an angled launch from a height, use y equals initial vertical velocity times t minus one half g t squared, and set y to the actual signed landing height. A quadratic can have two positive roots if the projectile passes a raised level once upward and again downward. The situation tells you which event is requested. There is one useful range result worth understanding: at fixed launch speed, with the same launch and landing height, range depends on sine of twice the launch angle. It is largest at forty-five degrees. Complementary angles have equal ranges but generally different flight times and heights. For different-height landing, neither that equal-range symmetry nor forty-five degrees as the optimum is generally valid. In JEE practice, first write the physical landing condition. Let the equation choose the time instead of making the scene fit a remembered shortcut.

chapters.title: Circular motion: direction is changing
chapters.formula: v = omega r; a(radial) = v^2/r; a(tangential) = dv/dt
points: Velocity is tangent; uniform circular acceleration points inward.
r = 2 m and v = 4 m/s: omega = 2 rad/s, period = pi s, radial acceleration = 8 m/s^2.
If tangential acceleration is 6 m/s^2, total acceleration magnitude is 10 m/s^2.
chapters.script: Constant speed does not always mean zero acceleration. Watch a point moving around a circle. At the rightmost point, an anticlockwise-moving point has upward velocity. A little later, its velocity tilts left. The speed can stay the same while the velocity vector changes direction. That change requires acceleration. For uniform circular motion, acceleration points toward the center, while velocity is tangent to the path. Over a very short interval, the little triangle formed by the velocity change is similar to the triangle formed by two nearby radius vectors. The magnitude of the velocity change divided by speed is approximately the traveled arc length divided by radius. Divide by the short time interval and take its limit. The inward acceleration becomes speed squared divided by radius. This is a kinematic result; a later force analysis identifies which real forces supply it. Angular speed omega means angle turned per second in radians. Arc length equals radius times angle, so speed equals omega times radius. One revolution covers two pi radians and takes a period of two pi divided by omega. Suppose radius is two meters and speed is four meters per second. Omega is two radians per second, period is pi seconds, and inward acceleration is eight meters per second squared. After half a revolution, distance traveled is two pi meters, but displacement magnitude is the diameter, four meters. Average speed remains four. Average velocity magnitude is displacement divided by half-period: eight divided by pi meters per second. Now let the point speed up. It still needs radial acceleration to turn, and it also has tangential acceleration to change speed. At the instant when speed is four and radius is two, radial acceleration is eight. If tangential acceleration is six, total acceleration magnitude is ten, from the square root of sixty-four plus thirty-six. The two components are perpendicular; their scalar magnitudes must not simply be added. Always use instantaneous speed in the radial formula. Uniform circular motion has constant angular speed, not constant velocity. That distinction is a common conceptual test.

chapters.title: Changing acceleration and the graph check
points: t in seconds, x in meters: differentiate position to get velocity and acceleration.
On 0 to 3 s, turning at 1 s: displacement = 0 m, distance = 8 m.
At 2 s: v = -3 m/s, a = 0; zero acceleration does not mean rest.
chapters.script: Let's finish with a problem that refuses to use constant acceleration. A particle's position in meters is t cubed minus six t squared plus nine t, with time in seconds. The numerical coefficients carry the corresponding SI units. We study time from zero to three seconds. Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the position-time graph, so differentiate position. Velocity is three t squared minus twelve t plus nine. Differentiate again: acceleration is six t minus twelve. Because acceleration changes with time, do not use the constant-acceleration equations over the whole journey. Factor the velocity as three times t minus one times t minus three. It is positive from zero to one second and negative from one to three. The particle turns around at one second. At three seconds it reaches zero velocity again, at our interval's endpoint. Now calculate position at the boundaries and at the interior turning point. Position at zero is zero. Position at one is four meters. Position at three is zero again. What is the total distance? Take a moment to separate it from displacement. The particle goes from zero to four, then from four back to zero: eight meters traveled. Displacement is zero. Its average velocity over three seconds is zero, but average speed is eight divided by three meters per second. The positive and negative areas under the velocity-time curve are plus four and minus four meters. That signed-area check agrees with the positions. At two seconds, acceleration is zero, but velocity is negative three meters per second. Zero acceleration at an instant does not mean rest. Before that instant, velocity and acceleration are both negative, so speed increases. After it, velocity is negative while acceleration is positive, so speed decreases. For a position graph, slope gives velocity; for a velocity graph, slope gives acceleration and signed area gives displacement. For an acceleration graph, signed area gives change in velocity, not displacement. This class adds the main missing motion models to our straight-line foundation. More multi-stage projectile, relative-motion and calculus practice still belongs in revision. Choose the frame, identify the acceleration model, solve the event condition, and then check the graph. That routine is far more dependable than hunting for a formula that merely looks familiar.

quiz.question: Trains of lengths 100 m and 140 m travel east at 18 and 12 m/s. From first overlap, full overtaking takes:
quiz.explanation: Relative travel is 100 + 140 = 240 m at 18 - 12 = 6 m/s: 40 s.

quiz.question: A boat aims north at 5 m/s relative to water. A 3 m/s east current flows across a 120 m-wide river. Drift is:
quiz.explanation: Northward crossing time is 120/5 = 24 s; eastward drift is 3 x 24 = 72 m.

quiz.question: The same boat lands directly opposite by canceling the 3 m/s current. Crossing time is:
quiz.explanation: The north component is sqrt(5^2 - 3^2) = 4 m/s, giving 120/4 = 30 s.

quiz.question: With no drag, u = 20 m/s at 30 degrees and g = 10 m/s^2. At the highest point, speed is:
quiz.explanation: Only vy is zero. vx = 20 cos(30 degrees) = 10 sqrt(3) m/s remains unchanged.

quiz.question: A horizontal launch at 15 m/s drops 20 m, with g = 10 m/s^2 and no drag. Impact speed is:
quiz.explanation: Falling time is 2 s; impact components are (15, -20) m/s. Speed is sqrt(225 + 400) = 25 m/s.

quiz.question: On a 2 m-radius circle at speed 4 m/s, tangential acceleration is 6 m/s^2. Total acceleration magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: Radial acceleration is 4^2/2 = 8. Perpendicular components give sqrt(8^2 + 6^2) = 10 m/s^2.

quiz.question: For x = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t in SI units, from t = 0 to 3 s, distance traveled is:
quiz.explanation: v = 3(t-1)(t-3). Positions are x(0)=0, x(1)=4, x(3)=0: distance 4 + 4 = 8 m.
